opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say it shaped almost everything I've worked on in recent years.

For a long time, my work was mostly on static images: classification, detection, network architecture design. Around the time of ResNet and after, there was real optimism that if we kept scaling data and models on ImageNet-style tasks, something like general visual intelligence would emerge, the way people later saw with language models. Gradually I came to feel that this wasn't happening, and the reason was quite fundamental.

In language, next-token prediction works so well because the data itself is a product of human thinking. Text is already highly compressed and abstract, so when a model learns to predict it, it's implicitly learning reasoning, knowledge, and structure. A static image is different. It's a record of the physical world, not of human cognition. You can train contrastive models, masked image models, generative models on images, and you do get good representations, but we never saw that clear emergent leap where scaling suddenly unlocks new abilities. Pixels alone don't carry the supervision signal for "thinking."

So my conclusion was that visual intelligence probably won't come from treating vision as a standalone problem of learning from images. It has to be connected to language, which gives you the abstraction, and ideally to temporal and interactive data like video and action, where causality and dynamics appear. That's why I moved toward multimodal large models: let language be the backbone of reasoning, and bring vision in as a deeply integrated part of the model, not a frozen encoder bolted on.

There's also a second, more subtle lesson. Even in multimodal models, understanding and generation have mostly been treated separately, and I think unifying them is still an open problem. If a model can truly understand an image, it should be able to reason about it, imagine changes to it, and predict what happens next. Getting there probably requires something like chain-of-thought in the visual domain, and possibly reinforcement learning on top, rather than only passive pre-training on static data.

So in short, recognizing the ceiling of static-image learning pushed me away from purely visual pre-training and toward a path where vision is grounded in language, time, and eventually interaction. I don't think we've solved it yet, but I'm much more confident that this is the right direction.

r002.rationale: It says language data is a product of human thinking and that text reflects human cognition, attributing language modeling’s strengths to the source of its training text.

r008.rationale: It does not cite a scarcity of detailed physical processes in internet image-text material as a reason to pursue video.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the turning point for me was realizing that for roughly a decade, almost everything we did in computer vision was really "learning from static images," and that this paradigm has a ceiling built into it that no amount of scaling can remove.

Look at what actually happened. From AlexNet through ResNet to the vision Transformers and CLIP-style models, the recipe was the same: take a huge pile of pictures, attach labels or captions, and train a network to compress the mapping. We got very good at it. Recognition basically got solved as a benchmark problem. But if you sit down and ask, "Does this model understand the world?", the honest answer is no. It understands the statistics of photographs. It knows that a cup usually appears on a table, that a cat has fur. It does not know that if you push the cup, it falls, or that the cat will move away if you reach for it. There is no notion of cause and effect, no notion of time, no notion of "I did something and the world changed."

The analogy I kept coming back to was language. Why did language models suddenly produce something that looked like intelligence, while vision models trained on far more pixels did not? My conclusion was that text is not a passive dataset. Text is the compressed trace of human reasoning and action. When you do next-token prediction on it, you are implicitly learning the dynamics of how humans think and act. A static image has no such temporal structure. You can predict masked pixels forever and you will learn textures and shapes, but you will never be forced to learn how the world evolves, because the data never shows it evolving.

So the limit was not about data volume or model size. It was that the learning signal itself was missing an axis. Images have no "next step." And intelligence, at least the kind we care about, is fundamentally about predicting and influencing what happens next.

Once I accepted that, the path became fairly clear, even if it was uncomfortable. First, the unit of learning has to be a sequence rather than a frame: video, and more importantly video coupled with actions, so the model sees the consequence of behavior. Second, the model should be generative and predictive in the temporal direction, not just discriminative on a snapshot. Third, and this is the part that pulled me toward embodiment and world models, the system has to be able to act, because without actions you cannot distinguish correlation from causation. An agent that can intervene gets a kind of supervision that passive viewing can never provide.

There was also a more personal lesson. I had spent years making static recognition networks more efficient and more accurate, and it was genuinely rewarding. But I started to feel that we were polishing the wrong objective. Being 0.5 percent better on a benchmark that measures the wrong thing is not progress toward visual intelligence. It was hard to let go of a direction that was working, but I think recognizing a ceiling early is more valuable than hitting it late.

So my current view is simple: static-image learning gave us excellent perception modules, and we should keep them. But visual intelligence will not emerge from them. It emerges when a model lives in time, predicts the future, and has its predictions corrected by acting in the world. That is why I moved from building better recognizers toward building systems that learn the dynamics of the physical world.

astra-6.text:
For me, static-image learning was an important starting point, but it also made the limits of recognition clear. A model can identify an object in a photograph without understanding how it moves, what caused its current state, or what would happen if you interacted with it. Recognizing something is only one part of understanding it.

That pushed my thinking toward visual intelligence grounded in change and interaction. Video introduces time: you can observe motion, persistence, and consequences. Interaction adds another dimension, because a system can act and see whether its expectations were correct. Neither automatically produces understanding, but both give us a richer setting in which to pursue it.

So the question became less “How accurately can we classify this image?” and more “What can a system learn about the world from seeing it, predicting what happens next, and acting within it?” Static images remain valuable, but I see them as a foundation for that broader goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I came to see static-image learning as an important starting point, but an incomplete account of visual intelligence. A single image tells you what a scene looks like at one moment. It gives you much less evidence about how that scene changes, why something moves, or what might happen next. A model can become very good at recognizing patterns without necessarily understanding those relationships.

That shaped the direction I wanted to pursue: moving from recognizing objects toward understanding a world that unfolds over time. Motion, interaction, and temporal context give us opportunities to learn things that are difficult to infer from isolated images. The question becomes not just “What is this?” but “What is happening, and how will it change?”

For me, that is a central step toward visual intelligence: building representations that support understanding and prediction, alongside recognition.
